title: The good of all beings
hookLine: twice the Gita describes people near the goal as delighting in the good of all beings
carry: delight in the good of all beings

lines: DELIGHTING IN THE GOOD OF ALL BEINGS.
SIX DAYS: A YEAR OF SERVICE.
cards: Sarvabhutahite ratah. A short Sanskrit phrase that turns up twice in the Gita, both times describing people who've come close to the goal. It means delighting in the good of all beings.
Over six days, we'll sketch a year of service. Today, the reason under the whole thing.

teach.h: CHAPTER FIVE: THE SAGES NEAR THE GOAL.
teach.b: First, in paraphrase: near the end of chapter five, Krishna describes the sages who reach the peace of Brahman: their faults worn away, their doubts cut through, their selves held steady, delighting in the good of all beings.
Then, in chapter twelve, Arjuna asks which worshipers know yoga better: those who love God with a form, or those who seek the imperishable, beyond form?

Krishna answers that those who fix their minds on him are the most devoted. But of the second group he says: with the senses held in, even-minded everywhere, delighting in the good of all beings, they too come to me.
The phrase sits not in a chapter on charity, not in a list of rules, but inside portraits of people near the end of the path.

teach.h: CARE AS A MARK OF COMING CLOSE.
teach.b: On this reading, care for others isn't only a road toward the goal. It's one of the marks of having come close to it. That gives seva, a word Hindus use for service, a particular root.
Not service as an extra on a free weekend but as something a settled heart is glad to do. And look at the word all. Not all who agree with me, not all in my family or my town.
All beings. Hindu homes have an old way of practicing that word.

teach.h: FOOD FOR THE BIRDS BEFORE BREAKFAST.
teach.b: The law books list five daily offerings a householder makes, and one of them is to the beings: a little food set out for birds, animals, whatever lives nearby.
It's why some grandmothers put out rice for the birds, or the first roti for a cow, before the family eats. A temple kitchen feeding whoever walks in is the same idea, bigger.
So a year of service can start before any calendar: whose good would you be glad to see, and how far past your own people can that circle reach?

how: Seva, selfless service, takes forms such as cooking and serving food at temples, caring for elders and guests, and cleaning shared spaces, and many Hindu homes keep the old daily offering to the beings: a little food set out for birds or animals before the family eats.

s: the phrase about the good of all beings appears only once in the Gita
it comes near the end of chapter five and again in chapter twelve.
both times, the phrase describes people near the goal of the path
the sages of chapter five and the seekers of the imperishable in chapter twelve.
the phrase asks for the good of one's own family only

games.q: Krishna is describing people who have come close to the goal. which mark does he name, in chapters five and twelve?
o: they have left all other people behind.
they delight in the good of all beings.
they care only for those who agree with them.
games.why: Gita 5.25 and 12.4 both describe them as sarvabhutahite ratah, delighting in the good of all beings.

practice: Bring to mind one person whose good you'd be glad to see today, then let the circle open one ring at a time, a neighbor, a coworker, a stranger in another city, an animal, a tree on your street, and notice where gladness gets harder, marking that place without pushing past it.
If you pray, you can hold the whole circle before the one you pray to.

wordCard.voice: Sarvabhutahite ratah. Delighting in the good of all beings, a phrase from the Gita, said of those near the path's end.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: sarvabhutahite ratah, delighting in the good of all beings, from Gita 5.25 and 12.4.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 5.25 (the sages who reach the peace of Brahman, delighting in the good of all beings)
Bhagavad Gita 12.1–12.4 (Arjuna's question; seekers of the imperishable, even-minded, delighting in the good of all beings, also reach Krishna)
Bhagavad Gita 3.20 (Janaka and lokasangraha, recalled from day 964)
